newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine to shut down Chernobyl reactor next month.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine to shut down Chernobyl reactor next month.

text.p: Ukraine on Monday vowed to close one of two working reactors at Chernobyl in November, sticking to a timetable agreed with Western donors to shut down the site of the world's worst nuclear disaster by the year 2000.
"On November 30 Reactor Number One will be stopped completely," Environment and Nuclear Safety Minister Yuri Kostenko told a news conference.
"Once reactor No. 1 has been stopped, Ukrainian scientists at Chernobyl will investigate the condition of the reactor and the best way to get the fuel out," he added.
Two weeks ago Kostenko said shutting down the reactor in October or November, as previously agreed by Ukrainian officials, could make the plant more prone to problems.
Chernobyl's fourth reactor exploded in 1986, sending a radioactive cloud across much of Europe, and Western nations have been urging Kiev ever since to shut down the whole site.
But apart from the fourth reactor, which is encased in a cracking concrete "sarcophagus," only one other reactor was stopped, after a fire in 1991.
Ukraine has accused the West of being slow to deliver $3 billion in grants and funding to help close Chernobyl, where about 5,000 people are still employed.
The former Soviet republic has payments problems not seen in rich nations, and the two remaining reactors have been supplying its 52 million people with five percent of their electricity.
Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, fearing an energy crisis this winter, threatened last week to stop supplying electricity to industries and factories which did not pay bills.
"Unfortunately we give away 47 percent of our electricity for free," Tatyana Yakysh, spokeswoman for the state Nuclear Authority Derzhkomatom, said.

Kostenko gave no indication of how the loss of power from reactor No. 1 would be compensated for in the short term and his pledge to stick by the agreed shut-down timetable seemed designed to please Western donors.

President Leonid Kuchma and his policy-making body, the Security Council, agreed at the weekend that the shut-down should go ahead as planned. "All participants agreed that the reactor should be stopped on the 30th," Kostenko said.
Kiev has agreed to close the plant down entirely this century in return for cash from the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development is expected to grant money to build two reactors at the Kmelnytsky and Rivne stations in western Ukraine to replace electricity lost by Chernobyl's closure.
Another concern has been the state of the concrete tomb around the wrecked reactor, where higher neutron readings were registered in September, sparking fears of a new explosion.

Kostenko said the United States would give $27 million by next September to help make the sarcophagus safer. "Our main task is to create a long-term funding mechanism to shut the Chernobyl station and put an end to the problem," he said.
Scientists said the higher readings were caused by rain seeping through the cracks and the State Nuclear Authority denied the situation had come anywhere near causing an accident.
